my dad taught me this at 5. The "3 rows of 7" trick is a classic, self-working magic trick using 21 cards. By having the spectator select a card and dealing the cards into three rows over three rounds—always placing the row with the chosen card in the middle—the selected card will mathematically land in the 11th position. [1, 2]
How to Perform the Trick

Deal the Cards: Count out exactly 21 cards from a standard deck. Deal them face-up into three horizontal rows of seven cards each (so you have three columns).
Make a Selection: Ask a spectator to mentally pick one card without telling you what it is.
Identify the Row: Ask the spectator which row contains their chosen card.
Gather and Repeat: Pick up the three rows. You must ensure that the row containing their chosen card is sandwiched in the middle of the other two rows.
Repeat Two More Times: Deal the cards out again into three rows of seven, ask which row holds their card, and pick them up again with the chosen row in the center. Do this dealing and stacking process exactly three times.
Reveal the Card: After the third pickup, the spectator's chosen card will always be the 11th card from the top of the pile. You can simply count down to the 11th card and dramatically flip it over to reveal it is their chosen card. [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

To read more about the mathematical probability and the algebra that powers this trick, check out the Mathematics behind this card trick discussion on Stack Exchange, or explore the Twenty-One Card Trick entry on Wikipedia. [1]

the beauty of it is how stupidly simple the method is while still feeling impossible to the person watching. you’re not doing any real “magic” — you’re just forcing the card into a known position through the way you stack the rows. every time they tell you which row it’s in, you’re getting one piece of information, and by always sandwiching that row in the middle, you’re slowly encoding its position in base 3. after three rounds you have enough information to know exactly where it is.

it’s one of those tricks that feels like it shouldn’t work, but the math is completely unforgiving. once you understand the mechanism, it stops being magic and becomes something closer to… an algorithm wearing a costume.
